title: Guru Hargobind: courage
hook: the sixth Guru's light: two swords, one heart
tomorrow: why did a Guru hold his robe close every time he walked?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan: sweet will, the plan breaks and the line holds. A new week opens at Simran's college orientation.

The orientation icebreaker is going badly in the usual way: name tags, a beach ball, a forced fun fact. A Sikh kid in Simran's group, quiet, patka on, catches the ball, and a guy across the circle says: nice tea towel. A few people laugh. Simran's loud laugh doesn't come. She stands up. She doesn't yell. She says: it's called a patka, his name is Gurpreet, and you'll learn it. The circle goes quiet. Later, still shaking, she texts you: was that too much? She's thinking of a Guru who wore two swords.
screen: `NAME TAGS AND A BEACH BALL.` → `NICE TEA TOWEL.` → `SHE STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells it this way. After his father, Guru Arjan, was killed in Lahore, the young Guru Hargobind did something new. He put on two swords. One was miri, worldly power: the duty to protect, to stand up in the world. The other was piri, spiritual authority: the inner life, the Name. Two swords, one heart. Facing the Harmandir Sahib he raised a seat, the Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless, where the Sikhs' worldly matters could be heard. Prayer and protection side by side, neither one alone. The Guru Granth Sahib has a picture of this kind of courage, in a verse of Kabir on Ang 1105. In paraphrase: the one who is truly brave fights for the helpless, and does not leave the field. Notice who the fight is for. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: in Amritsar, tradition says, the seat of worldly duty was built facing the seat of prayer, so each stays in sight of the other. Simran's version was small: one sentence, no shove. She stood up, and she kept it clean. After the session, the guy finds Gurpreet and asks how to say his name right.
screen: `TWO SWORDS: MIRI AND PIRI.` · `THE AKAL TAKHT, FACING THE PRAYER.` · `BRAVE FOR THE HELPLESS.` · `ONE SENTENCE, NO SHOVE.` · then, large: `COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, feet under your hips, and let your spine grow tall, shoulders back and soft. Rest one hand over your heart and let the other hang loose at your side, one for the inner life and one for the world. Breathe slowly in this stance until the sit ends.
Guru Hargobind: the sixth Guru, who wore two swords, miri and piri. Courage in the world, and the Name inside it.
The line for today: courage, two swords and one heart, brave for someone else. A new week, standing.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind as the Guru of miri and piri; the Akal Takht in Amritsar, across from the Harmandir Sahib, is a seat of Sikh authority, and the two swords appear in the Sikh emblem, the khanda.
